change.before: Supplied by the vasa vasorum of its wall in the neck and by the caroticotympanic and capsular branches intracranially; the cavernous segment is surrounded by the cavernous sinus and its nerves, and the supraclinoid segment by the subarachnoid space, which is why aneurysms here bleed into the subarachnoid space or into the sinus.
change.after: Inflow from the common carotid artery. Through its ACA, MCA, anterior choroidal and communicating branches it supplies variable cortical and deep territories; a fetal PCA configuration can extend the carotid territory into the occipital lobe.

before.findings: Occlusion of the internal carotid produces the largest infarcts of all — a combined ACA/MCA territory deficit with contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia, hemianopia, gaze deviation and (dominant hemisphere) global aphasia; embolism from an atherosclerotic plaque at the bifurcation is the usual mechanism, and the deficit may be stepwise rather than sudden.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery (with middle cerebral artery territory dominance)

before.syndrome: Amaurosis fugax and ocular ischaemic syndrome
before.findings: Transient monocular blindness ('a curtain coming down') from emboli to the ophthalmic/retinal circulation, or chronic hypoperfusion of the eye with venous stasis retinopathy — a direct marker of ipsilateral carotid stenosis.
before.vascular: Ophthalmic artery (first branch of the internal carotid) from an internal carotid plaque

before.findings: A cavernous-carotid aneurysm or fistula compresses cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI within the sinus, producing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, facial sensory loss in the first two divisions, a pulsatile bruit and (with a fistula) proptosis and chemosis with arterialized conjunctival veins.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery (cavernous segment) — the segment whose wall IS the sinus

before.findings: A tear in the cervical internal-carotid wall (spontaneous, traumatic or connective-tissue related) creates an intramural haematoma with ipsilateral neck/face pain, Horner syndrome, pulsatile tinnitus and a risk of embolism, especially in patients under 50.
before.vascular: Internal carotid artery (cervical segment)

after.findings: Clinical extent ranges from no deficit with effective collateral flow to retinal ischaemia, MCA-predominant infarction, watershed injury or a combined ACA/MCA infarction. Possible findings include contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss, with aphasia in a language-dominant hemisphere or neglect in the other hemisphere.
after.vascular: Internal carotid artery and its branches

after.findings: Transient monocular visual loss can result from ipsilateral carotid embolism or hypoperfusion of the retinal circulation; carotid disease is one of several possible causes.

after.syndrome: Cavernous ICA aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula
after.findings: Compression can affect ocular motor nerves and V1/V2 sensation. A fistula may cause proptosis, chemosis, pulsatile bruit and arterialized conjunctival veins. The cavernous ICA is extradural; haemorrhage patterns differ from intradural aneurysms.
May cause ipsilateral head or neck pain, partial Horner syndrome and cerebral or retinal ischaemia from thromboembolism or reduced flow.

change.reason: Correct cavernous relationships, variable clinical extent, and Heubner origin; replace unsupported vessel-wall supply with arterial inflow.
change.before: The anterior feeding trunk of the cerebral circulation: it enters the skull through the carotid canal, runs through the cavernous sinus (where it is related to cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI) and turns upward and backward through the dural ring to become the supraclinoid segment, giving off the ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries before dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries at the carotid bifurcation. Its four segments (cervical, petrous, cavernous, supraclinoid) each generate a distinct syndrome, and together with the vertebrobasilar system it completes the circle of Willis at the base of the brain.
change.after: Paired source of the anterior cerebral circulation. After cervical and petrous segments, the ICA passes through the cavernous sinus, then enters the subarachnoid space as the supraclinoid segment. CN VI and sympathetic fibres lie beside the cavernous ICA; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the sinus lateral wall. Major distal branches are the ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries, followed by the terminal ACA and MCA. These four segment names are a teaching simplification of more detailed segment classifications.

change.reason: V1 is preforaminal; medullary arteries and consequences vary.
change.before: Its wall is supplied by the vasa vasorum of the periosteal and dural sleeves along the cervical loop; the V4 segment lies in the subarachnoid space in front of the medulla, where it is adjacent to the hypoglossal rootlets, the vertebral venous plexus and the lower cranial nerves.
change.after: Inflow from the subclavian artery; distal branches include medullary perforators, anterior/posterior spinal branches and usually PICA.

fieldAudit.assessment: V1 is preforaminal; medullary arteries and consequences vary. Clinical patterns depend on actual lesion extent; the rendered route is not sufficient to diagnose a vascular syndrome.

change.reason: V1 is preforaminal; medullary arteries and consequences vary.

before.findings: Vertebral artery occlusion at the origin of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts the dorsolateral medulla: vertigo, nystagmus, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ataxia, loss of pain-temperature on the ipsilateral face and the contralateral body, dysphagia, hoarseness and diminished gag reflex with intact strength.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery at the PICA origin (or the PICA itself)

before.findings: Infarction of the paramedian medullary territory supplied by the anterior spinal/vertebral arteries produces contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid) sparing the face, contralateral loss of position and vibration sense (medial lemniscus) and ipsilateral tongue weakness (hypoglossal nerve) — the classic alternating brainstem syndrome.
before.vascular: Anterior spinal artery or paramedian vertebral branches

before.syndrome: Vertebral artery dissection and subarachnoid haemorrhage
before.findings: Cervical dissection causes posterior-circulation transient ischaemic attacks and stroke in young adults with neck pain and occipital headache; rupture of an intracranial vertebral aneurysm fills the subarachnoid space around the brainstem and can present with a devastating brainstem infarct.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery (cervical segment for dissection, V4 for aneurysm)

before.findings: Occlusion or compression of the contralateral vertebral artery with head rotation (a variant of the atlantoaxial anatomy) causes vertigo, diplopia and syncope on turning the head.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery (V2/V3 segment at the atlantoaxial level)

after.findings: A lateral medullary infarct can produce ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral ataxia and Horner syndrome, vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia and hoarseness. The full constellation is not required, and vertebral or PICA disease can be responsible.
Paramedian injury can combine contralateral weakness and vibration-position loss with ipsilateral hypoglossal weakness. The triad is often incomplete.
after.vascular: Paramedian vertebral branches rostrally and anterior spinal branches more caudally

after.findings: May produce head/neck pain and posterior circulation ischaemia. Intracranial dissections can also rupture into the subarachnoid space.

change.reason: V1 is preforaminal; medullary arteries and consequences vary.
change.before: The paired feeding trunk of the posterior circulation: each artery ascends through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae (V1/V2), loops laterally behind the atlas and then pierces the dura to run upward and medially in front of the medulla (V4). Its branches supply the cervical cord, the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum, and the two vertebral arteries unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery — the union being the last point where the posterior circulation is still paired.
change.after: Paired arteries arising from the subclavian arteries. V1 runs to the transverse foramen, V2 usually ascends through C6-C2 transverse foramina, V3 curves around the atlas, and V4 passes through the dura and foramen magnum to the ventral medulla. The vertebral arteries usually unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. Medullary, spinal and PICA branches provide variable supply to the medulla, upper cord and inferior cerebellum.

change.reason: Remove invariant complete pontine destruction and unneeded treatment claim; distinguish ventral/dorsal territories.
change.before: Its wall is supplied by small vasa vasorum from the pontine perforators; the artery lies within the prepontine cistern, surrounded by CSF, which is why aneurysms of its apex present with subarachnoid haemorrhage and a third-nerve palsy, and why the basilar apex is the classic target of endovascular thrombectomy in acute basilar occlusion.
change.after: Inflow from both vertebral arteries; branches supply the pons and contribute to cerebellar, midbrain and posterior cerebral circulation. Communicating-artery collateral flow is variable.

fieldAudit.assessment: Remove invariant complete pontine destruction and unneeded treatment claim; distinguish ventral/dorsal territories. Clinical patterns depend on actual lesion extent; the rendered route is not sufficient to diagnose a vascular syndrome.

change.reason: Remove invariant complete pontine destruction and unneeded treatment claim; distinguish ventral/dorsal territories.

before.findings: Occlusion of the basilar artery with infarction of the basis pontis but sparing of the tegmentum leaves the patient conscious with intact vertical eye movements and blinking but completely paralysed and anarthric — quadriplegia, aphonia and preserved awareness, often misdiagnosed as coma.
before.vascular: Basilar artery (paramedian pontine perforators, basis pontis)

before.findings: A dorsal pontine lesion involving the paramedian pontine reticular formation and the adjacent medial longitudinal fasciculus abolishes horizontal gaze to one side and adduction on the other, leaving abduction with nystagmus in the only surviving direction; brainstem infarction (basilar perforators or a small tegmental haemorrhage) is the commonest cause.
before.vascular: Basilar artery paramedian perforators (dorsal caudal pons)

before.findings: Ventral pontine infarction produces an alternating syndrome: ipsilateral facial weakness (facial nucleus/nerve) or conjugate gaze palsy (abducens nucleus/PPRF) with contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal tract) and, in the full Foville form, contralateral sensory loss (medial lemniscus).
before.vascular: Basilar artery paramedian perforators (caudal pons), sometimes the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

before.findings: Embolic occlusion of the basilar apex infarcts the midbrain, thalamus and occipital cortex together: somnolence, peduncular hallucinosis, vertical gaze palsy, pupillary abnormality, memory loss and cortical blindness with relative sparing of motor function.
before.vascular: Basilar artery apex (with posterior cerebral artery territory)

after.findings: Bilateral ventral pontine injury can cause quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved awareness; vertical eye movements and blinking are often retained in the classic form. Basilar occlusion can also cause impaired consciousness or other syndromes when the tegmentum is affected.

A unilateral dorsal pontine lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus plus the ipsilateral MLF causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia; the other eye can still abduct. Infarction is one possible cause.

Caudal pontine lesions can combine ipsilateral facial or abducens dysfunction with contralateral weakness; dorsal extension may add gaze palsy and sensory loss. Findings depend on the actual lesion rather than on an eponym alone.

Distal basilar disease can affect variable combinations of rostral midbrain, thalami, occipital and medial temporal regions, causing altered consciousness, eye movement abnormalities, memory impairment and visual deficits.

change.before: The single midline trunk of the posterior circulation, formed at the pontomedullary junction by the union of the two vertebral arteries and running in the prepontine cistern along the ventral surface of the pons to divide into the two posterior cerebral arteries at the interpeduncular fossa. It supplies the whole basis pontis through crowded paramedian and circumferential perforators, gives off the anterior inferior cerebellar arteries and the superior cerebellar arteries, and its paramedian branches feed the medial lemniscus, the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres, the abducens nucleus, the paramedian pontine reticular formation and the cranial-nerve nuclei of the pons — so its occlusion can destroy the entire ventral brainstem at once.
change.after: Single trunk formed by the vertebral arteries near the pontomedullary junction. It runs in the prepontine cistern along the ventral pons, gives paramedian and circumferential pontine branches, AICA and SCA, and usually divides into the PCAs. Different branches supply ventral pontine motor pathways and dorsal or lateral tegmental structures; the extent of injury from basilar disease depends on the occlusion site and collateral circulation.

change.before: The largest and clinically most important cerebral artery: it runs laterally through the sylvian fissure (M1, giving off the lenticulostriate perforators), over the insula (M2 insular branches) and out onto the lateral convexity (M3/M4), supplying the entire lateral surface of the hemisphere — the motor and sensory strips for the face and arm, Broca's and Wernicke's areas, the insula, the temporal convexity and the lateral occipital cortex. change.after: Major ICA terminal artery. M1 travels laterally toward the Sylvian fissure and gives deep lenticulostriate perforators; insular M2, opercular M3 and cortical M4 branches supply most of the lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex and underlying white matter. ACA and PCA territories border this distribution, so the entire lateral surface is not uniformly MCA territory. Superior/inferior division anatomy is variable.

before.findings: An aneurysm at the carotid-posterior communicating junction compresses the oculomotor nerve where it passes beside the vessel: a painful, pupil-involving third-nerve palsy with ptosis, a divergent eye and diplopia — the classic 'posterior communicating' presentation, and one of the few genuinely urgent diplopias.

before.findings: Occlusion of the premammillary perforators infarcts the anterior thalamic nuclei and gives the tuberothalamic syndrome: apathy and abulia, disorientation, memory loss and, on the left, a transcortical-like aphasia.

before.findings: A small infarct of the subthalamic nucleus — classically from a perforator of the posterior communicating or anterior choroidal artery — releases the indirect-pathway brake and produces violent, involuntary, proximal flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery or anterior choroidal artery perforators to the subthalamic nucleus

before.syndrome: Fetal-type posterior communicating artery and posterior-circulation infarction
before.findings: In about 20 % of people the posterior cerebral artery is supplied predominantly by the internal carotid through a large posterior communicating artery; in that configuration carotid occlusion infarcts the occipital lobe and thalamus as well as the anterior territory — the reason the vascular anatomy must be established before any carotid intervention.
before.vascular: Posterior communicating artery (fetal-type configuration of the posterior cerebral artery)
before.note: Anatomical variant that changes the territory of a carotid occlusion

after.syndrome: ICA-PCoA aneurysm with CN III palsy
after.findings: An aneurysm can compress the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, producing ptosis, diplopia, impaired adduction/elevation/depression and often pupillary dilation. Pupil sparing does not by itself exclude compression.
Can cause disorientation, memory disturbance, abulia and sometimes dominant-hemisphere language impairment; territory varies with anterior thalamic arterial anatomy.
Injury to motor basal ganglia circuitry can cause contralateral hemichorea/hemiballismus; the responsible lesion need not be confined to the STN.
Carotid embolism may cause PCA cortical infarction because the carotid is the dominant inflow to that PCA. This is an anatomical variant, not itself a disease.

change.before: The artery of the visual cortex and the posterior diencephalon: it arises from the basilar bifurcation, curves around the midbrain (P2) and divides into the calcarine, parieto-occipital and posterior temporal branches (P3) that supply the medial and inferior occipital lobe, the medial temporal lobe and the posterior thalamus, while its paramedian and thalamogeniculate perforators supply the midbrain tectum and tegmentum, the thalamus and the medial geniculate body. Cortical and deep deficits depend on which branches are affected, and fetal PCA anatomy alters inflow.

before.findings: Vertigo, nausea and nystagmus (vestibular nuclei), ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss (spinal trigeminal), contralateral body pain and temperature loss (spinothalamic tract), dysphagia, hoarseness and absent gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic fibres), ipsilateral limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle) and impaired taste (solitary nucleus) — with strength, vibration sense and consciousness spared.
before.vascular: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (or the vertebral artery at its origin)

before.syndrome: PICA territory cerebellar infarct with oedema
before.findings: A large cerebellar infarct can obstruct the fourth ventricle and compress the brainstem, producing hydrocephalus, impaired consciousness and brainstem signs — the indication for posterior fossa decompression, and the reason a 'benign' lateral medullary syndrome is monitored for deterioration.
before.vascular: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (with mass effect)

before.findings: Aneurysms of the vertebral-PICA junction present with sudden headache, meningism and, frequently, a lateral medullary deficit from mass effect or vasospasm.
before.vascular: Vertebral artery / posterior inferior cerebellar artery junction

after.findings: Can cause ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ataxia and Horner syndrome with vertigo, dysphagia and hoarseness. Strength is often preserved, but extensions and incomplete patterns occur. Vertebral disease is also an important cause.
Vertigo, nausea and gait/limb ataxia may occur. A large infarct can cause fourth-ventricular obstruction or brainstem compression as it swells.
A proximal or distal PICA aneurysm may rupture into the subarachnoid space, sometimes with intraventricular blood; associated deficits depend on haemorrhage and neighbouring tissue injury.

change.before: The artery of the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellar surface: it arises from the vertebral artery (occasionally from the basilar) and makes a characteristic caudal loop around the tonsil before supplying the inferior vermis, the inferior cerebellar hemisphere and the dorsolateral medulla. Because its medullary branches supply the vestibular nuclei, the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, the nucleus ambiguus, the solitary nucleus, the inferior cerebellar peduncle, the spinothalamic tract and the descending sympathetic fibres in one territory, its occlusion produces the single most famous brainstem stroke syndrome — and it is also the artery whose absence must be checked before vertebral sacrifice.
change.after: Usually arises from the vertebral artery. Its variable course wraps around the medulla and cerebellar tonsil to the inferior vermis and hemisphere. The commonly described five segments are anterior medullary, lateral medullary, tonsillomedullary, telovelotonsillar and cortical. Medullary perforators share lateral medullary supply with vertebral branches; distal branches also supply fourth-ventricular choroid plexus.

before.findings: Rupture of a lateral lenticulostriate artery causes sudden contralateral hemiplegia and hemisensory loss with gaze deviation toward the lesion and, when large, depressed consciousness and transtentorial herniation — the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.
before.vascular: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries (middle cerebral artery)

before.syndrome: Lacunar infarction with a pure motor or pure sensory syndrome
before.findings: Lipohyalinosis of a single perforator produces a small infarct in the internal capsule, corona radiata or pons: a pure motor hemiparesis, a pure sensory stroke, ataxic hemiparesis or a dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome — with no cortical signs (no aphasia, no neglect, no field defect).
before.vascular: Lenticulostriate or other deep perforating arteries (small-vessel disease)

before.findings: Repeated, stereotyped episodes of pure motor or sensorimotor deficit that resolve within minutes, followed by a permanent lacunar infarct in the same territory — a stuttering occlusion of a single lenticulostriate artery that must be recognized as impending stroke.
before.vascular: A single lenticulostriate perforator (middle cerebral artery)

before.findings: Bleeding from the caudothalamic groove perforators ruptures into the lateral ventricle, producing headache, meningism, a reduced level of consciousness and hydrocephalus rather than a focal hemiplegia.
before.vascular: Medial lenticulostriate and Heubner territory perforators

after.findings: A small capsular lesion may cause pure motor or sensorimotor deficits, ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria-clumsy hand without typical cortical signs. Pure sensory stroke classically localizes to thalamic rather than lenticulostriate territory.
after.vascular: Striate / other deep perforators according to location

after.findings: Hypertension-related small-vessel injury can cause basal ganglia haemorrhage with contralateral weakness or sensory loss; large haemorrhages may extend into ventricles or cause mass effect.

Meshes: no dedicated BP3D concept exists. The nearest elements are the anterolateral central branches of the middle cerebral artery (`FJ1662`/`FJ1662M`, `FJ1663`/`FJ1663M`, FMA 50376–50378), which the inventory files as MCA `half+support` rather than as their own record; the remaining lenticulostriate elements are inside its 44-element "generic MCA branch/zone" group. The record is therefore documented as a two-vessel functional concept whose geometry the render task takes from the MCA branch set.

fieldAudit.assessment: Differentiate umbrella concept, limited collateralization, thalamic pure sensory localization and Heubner origin.

change.reason: Differentiate umbrella concept, limited collateralization, thalamic pure sensory localization and Heubner origin.
change.before: The deep perforating arteries that supply the basal ganglia and the internal capsule: the lateral group arises from the proximal (M1) middle cerebral artery and pierces the anterior perforated substance to run through the putamen to the internal capsule, while the medial group (including the recurrent artery of Heubner) arises from the anterior cerebral artery and supplies the caudate head, the nucleus accumbens and the anterior limb of the capsule. They are end arteries — there are no anastomoses at their destinations — and they are the vessels of lacunar infarction and of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, which is why the same anatomy explains both the commonest ischaemic and the commonest haemorrhagic deep lesion.
change.after: Umbrella term for striate perforators supplying parts of the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Lateral lenticulostriate branches usually arise from proximal MCA; medial striate branches arise from ACA, with the recurrent artery of Heubner usually near the ACA-ACoA junction or proximal A2. Deep perforator territories have limited collateralization and are vulnerable to small-vessel infarction or haemorrhage. The separate lateral and medial records provide group detail; the model does not encode a universal branch count.

change.before: Supplied by its parent carotid trunk; the artery runs in the ambient cistern below the optic tract, immediately above the posterior communicating artery, and is at risk during temporal-lobe surgery, aneurysm clipping and choroid plexus surgery (its injury causes an infarct of the internal capsule and a post-operative hemiplegia).
change.after: Inflow usually from the ICA. Cisternal branches supply deep neural tissue; plexal branches supply choroid plexus, not the CSF cavity itself.

fieldAudit.assessment: Qualify overlapping territory and incomplete triad; cavity is not perfused tissue. Clinical patterns depend on actual lesion extent; the rendered route is not sufficient to diagnose a vascular syndrome.

before.syndrome: Anterior choroidal artery infarct (the capsular triad)
before.findings: Contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia occur together because the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the thalamocortical sensory fibres and the optic radiation all fall within the territory; the incomplete forms (pure motor, pure sensory, or a quadrantanopia alone) are more common than the full triad.
before.vascular: Anterior choroidal artery

before.syndrome: Hippocampal and amygdalar infarction with memory loss
before.findings: Involvement of the uncal, hippocampal and amygdalar branches adds a memory deficit and, occasionally, seizures to the capsular findings — the anatomical reason the anterior choroidal territory appears in the clinical notes of the amygdala, hippocampus and temporal horn.
before.vascular: Anterior choroidal artery (cisternal branches)

before.syndrome: Anterior choroidal aneurysm and surgical risk
before.findings: Aneurysms of the anterior choroidal artery are rare but their clipping risks the artery itself; because it is an end-artery territory with no useful anastomoses, occlusion during surgery produces an immediate, dense capsular hemiplegia.
before.vascular: Anterior choroidal artery (iatrogenic occlusion)

after.findings: The classical combination is contralateral weakness, sensory loss and homonymous field loss; partial syndromes are common and depend on capsular and visual pathway involvement.

The artery can be at risk during aneurysm or medial temporal/intraventricular procedures. Occlusion can injure eloquent deep tissue; outcome is variable rather than invariably a complete dense hemiplegia.

change.before: A small but surgically notorious artery arising from the internal carotid just above the posterior communicating artery: it runs backward below the optic tract, gives off the uncal, hippocampal and pallidal branches, and enters the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle through the choroidal fissure to supply the choroid plexus. Its territory is a compact bundle of functionally unrelated structures — the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic radiation (retrolenticular part), the globus pallidus, the hippocampus, the amygdala, the tail of the caudate and the temporal-horn plexus — which is why its occlusion produces the 'capsular triad' of hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia rather than a single clean syndrome.
change.after: Usually arises from the supraclinoid ICA distal to the PCoA and courses posteriorly near the optic tract before entering the choroidal fissure/temporal horn plexus. Supplies variable parts of the posterior internal capsule, optic tract/geniculocalcarine pathway, pallidum and medial temporal structures, and lateral-ventricular choroid plexus. Individual territory overlaps neighbouring perforators and choroidal arteries.

before.findings: Choroid plexus papillomas and carcinomas, and intraventricular meningiomas of the trigone, are fed by the posterior choroidal arteries (and the anterior choroidal artery anteriorly); recognizing the pedicle is what makes embolization and surgical control possible.
before.vascular: Posterior choroidal arteries (with the anterior choroidal artery)

before.findings: Occlusion produces infarction of the posterior thalamus and the adjacent plexus, adding hemisensory loss, visual field defects and memory disturbance to the picture of a posterior cerebral artery infarct; isolated occlusion is uncommon because the artery arises from the PCA itself.
before.vascular: Posterior cerebral artery (posterior choroidal branches)

before.syndrome: Intraventricular haemorrhage from the choroidal vessels
before.findings: The choroidal arteries are the source of intraventricular haemorrhage in the premature (germinal matrix) and of blood in the ventricles in adults with hypertension or vascular malformation; blood in the ventricle is what produces hydrocephalus.
before.vascular: Choroidal arteries (with the germinal matrix in neonates)

after.findings: Injury may affect thalamic/epithalamic tissue or choroid plexus depending on the branches involved. Exact sensory, visual or memory findings cannot be inferred from this single schematic course.

after.findings: Can cause contralateral homonymous field loss. Macular sparing may occur through preserved cortex or collateral supply, but is not universal. Bilateral cortical injury can impair vision with preserved pupillary light responses.

before.syndrome: Locked-in syndrome (basilar occlusion with perforator loss)
before.findings: Occlusion of the basilar trunk removes all the paramedian perforators at once and infarcts the whole basis pontis while sparing the tegmentum: the patient is conscious, blinks and moves the eyes vertically but is otherwise quadriplegic and anarthric. It is the most devastating expression of a perforator territory and the reason the basilar is treated as an emergency.
before.vascular: Basilar artery and its pontine perforating arteries

before.findings: A single paramedian pontine perforator infarct produces a small lacune in the basis pontis: a pure motor hemiparesis contralateral to the lesion, without sensory loss, aphasia or visual field defect, and often with a dysarthriaâ€“clumsy hand picture when the lesion sits more rostrally. It is clinically indistinguishable from a capsular lacune, which is why imaging is required.
before.vascular: Basilar artery pontine perforating arteries

before.findings: A slightly larger paramedian or short circumferential infarct reaches the facial nucleus or the abducens nucleus and PPRF, producing the alternating syndromes: ipsilateral facial weakness (or conjugate gaze palsy) with contralateral hemiparesis, and in the Foville form a contralateral sensory loss from medial lemniscus involvement.

after.findings: Can cause pure motor weakness, ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria-clumsy hand; tegmental extension adds gaze or cranial nerve signs. Bilateral ventral pontine injury can cause locked-in syndrome, but basilar occlusion does not invariably spare the tegmentum.

before.syndrome: Lacunar infarction of the internal capsule and basal ganglia
before.findings: Occlusion of one lateral lenticulostriate artery infarcts a small deep territory: pure motor stroke (posterior limb, corticospinal fibres), pure sensory stroke (thalamocapsular fibres), ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria–clumsy hand. There is no aphasia, no neglect, no hemianopia and no drowsiness — the cortex is untouched, which is the clinical signature of a deep perforator lesion. NOTE: this atlas has no dedicated lacunar-syndrome card in src/data/syndromes, so `supply` is empty by the honesty rule rather than by oversight; the clinical picture is documented here and in the four child records.
before.vascular: Lateral lenticulostriate arteries (middle cerebral artery M1 perforators)

before.findings: Rupture of a Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysm on a lenticulostriate artery fills the putamen and spreads along the internal capsule into the ventricle: sudden contralateral hemiplegia with conjugate gaze deviation, depressed consciousness and, with a large clot, transtentorial herniation. It is the commonest site of spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage.

before.findings: When several lenticulostriate arteries occlude at once — typically by an embolus lodging at the M1 bifurcation or by a carotid occlusion with poor collateral flow — the infarct becomes a large striatocapsular cavity with hemiplegia and, on the left, a cortical-like aphasia from the adjacent insular and opercular involvement. A clinical syndrome with gait impairment, cognitive difficulty and urinary symptoms associated with ventriculomegaly. The full triad is not required and one normal pressure measurement is not diagnostic; ventricular size alone cannot distinguish it from atrophy.

Mild asymmetry can be a normal variant. Interpretation requires surrounding tissue, obstruction and clinical context, rather than a horn-size rule alone.

change.before: The paired C-shaped CSF space of the cerebral hemisphere: its body lies under the corpus callosum with the caudate above the thalamus, and its frontal, temporal and occipital horns extend into the three lobes around the thalamus. It hosts the choroid plexus that produces most of the CSF it contains and drains through the interventricular foramen of Monro into the third ventricle, and thence through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle — the atrium and the temporal and occipital horns are terminal recesses of the same compartment, so its shape is a direct readout of the deep hemispheric anatomy.
change.after: Paired C-shaped CSF cavities within the cerebral hemispheres. The frontal horn lies anterior to the foramen of Monro, the body continues posteriorly under the corpus callosum, and the atrium joins body with occipital and temporal horns. Each lateral ventricle communicates with the third ventricle through its own interventricular foramen. Plexus is present in the body, atrium and temporal horn, not the frontal or occipital horn.

Small cysts at the glomus are common and almost always incidental in adults; in fetuses they are a soft marker that resolves in most cases.

Normal choroid plexus enhances because its capillaries are fenestrated. Abnormal enhancement may occur with inflammation or tumor, but enhancement alone does not diagnose infection.

change.before: The villous, fenestrated capillary-CSF interface that secretes the great majority of the cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood-CSF barrier: it extends from the interventricular foramen along the body and atrium into the temporal horn, but is absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Its epithelial tight junctions, carbonic anhydrase activity and aquaporin-1 expression make CSF production a regulated, energy-dependent process — and the target of acetazolamide.
change.after: Vascular villous tissue projecting into the ventricular body, atrium and temporal horn, absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Choroid epithelium actively secretes much of the CSF and its tight junctions form the blood-CSF barrier; the capillaries themselves are fenestrated. It connects with the third-ventricular plexus near the interventricular foramen.

before.syndrome: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
before.findings: A cyst impacted at the foramen of Monro causes intermittent positional headache, drop attacks and acute hydrocephalus with dilated lateral ventricles and a normal-sized third ventricle, and is a recognized cause of sudden death.
before.vascular: Not vascular — mechanical obstruction at the foramen

before.findings: Obstruction of one foramen (tumour, cyst, ventriculitis, shunt malfunction) dilates only that lateral ventricle, shifting the septum pellucidum across the midline.
before.note: Obstructive — the asymmetry itself identifies the level of the block

before.findings: A enhancing mass at the foramen of Monro in a patient with tuberous sclerosis obstructs CSF flow and is one of the major diagnostic criteria for the disease.
before.note: Genetic/hamartomatous; the location makes it symptomatic

after.findings: A lesion near Monro can obstruct one or both lateral ventricles, sometimes causing intermittent or acute hydrocephalus. Sudden deterioration is possible but not the usual course of every small cyst.
One blocked foramen can produce predominantly ipsilateral lateral-ventricular enlargement; ventricular asymmetry alone does not prove obstruction.
A subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis or another intraventricular mass may obstruct CSF flow. Imaging and disease context are needed for diagnosis.

before.syndrome: Central neurocytoma (foramen of Monro/body of the lateral ventricle)
before.findings: A calcified, enhancing intraventricular mass attached to the septum pellucidum at the level of the foramen of Monro in a young adult causes intermittent obstructive hydrocephalus and headache; it is the classic tumour of the ventricular body in this age group.
before.vascular: Choroidal feeders (anterior/posterior choroidal arteries) at surgery

before.syndrome: Thalamostriate vein displacement as a mass sign
before.findings: On coronal imaging the thalamostriate vein and the internal cerebral vein form the venous angle at the foramen of Monro; their displacement distinguishes an intraventricular mass (displacing the vein laterally) from a thalamic mass (displacing it medially).
before.note: Imaging localizing sign rather than a disease

before.findings: Tumour cells and infection spread along the ependyma of the body and the subependymal plate, producing linear enhancement; the same subependymal germinal matrix is the origin of periventricular nodular heterotopia and the site of germinal-matrix haemorrhage at the caudothalamic groove.

Because the body is bounded above by the corpus callosum and below by the thalamus, its disproportionate enlargement with an upgoing third ventricle on sagittal MRI is the hallmark of aqueductal stenosis, and it produces the 'Mickey Mouse' appearance of the frontal horns on axial imaging.

after.findings: Central neurocytoma often attaches near the septum pellucidum/foramen region and may obstruct CSF. Calcification and enhancement can support a differential diagnosis but histopathology establishes tumor type.

Tumor or infection can involve the ependymal/subependymal region; abnormal enhancement is nonspecific. Developmental heterotopia and premature-infant germinal-matrix haemorrhage have different mechanisms and should not be treated as the same disorder.
Can accompany upstream CSF obstruction or tissue-volume loss. Aqueductal stenosis typically enlarges lateral/third ventricles; no body shape alone is a specific diagnostic hallmark.

change.before: The central part of the lateral ventricle — the long horizontal segment between the frontal horn (at the interventricular foramen) and the atrium, roofed by the body of the corpus callosum and floored by the thalamus medially and the caudate nucleus laterally, with the choroid plexus running along its floor through the choroidal fissure. It is the segment that defines the thalamostriate groove: the thalamostriate vein and the stria terminalis mark the caudothalamic junction along its floor, the vein of Galen's tributaries (internal cerebral veins) run in the tela choroidea above the thalamus, and the subependymal venous angle at the foramen of Monro is the surgical landmark for the anterior third ventricle. Its width and the height of the corpus callosum above it are the standard measures of ventricular enlargement.
change.after: Central portion posterior to the foramen of Monro and anterior to the atrium, roofed by the corpus callosum. Floor relations include caudate body laterally and thalamus more medially, separated by the stria terminalis/thalamostriate region; fornix and septum pellucidum contribute medially. Choroid plexus lies along the choroidal fissure. This describes gross relationships, not precise boundaries in every specimen.
